content: Herpes labialis, also referred to as orolabial herpes, is an infection of the lip caused by the herpes simplex virus (HSV). This condition often results in the formation of small blisters or sores around the mouth, commonly known as cold sores or fever blisters. It is important to note that the term labialis refers to the lips and does not pertain to the genital labia, despite the shared etymology. When the herpes simplex virus infects both the face and mouth, the broader term orofacial herpes is used. If the infection specifically involves the mouth, it is referred to as herpetic stomatitis, derived from the Greek word stoma, meaning mouth. The sores associated with herpes labialis typically heal within 2 to 3 weeks. However, the virus remains in the body and becomes dormant in the facial nerves. Periodically, the virus may reactivate, causing recurrent sores in the same area of the mouth or face as the initial infection. Herpes labialis occurs when the herpes simplex virus comes into contact with oral mucosal tissue or abraded skin around the mouth. The type 1 strain of herpes simplex virus (HSV-1) is the most common cause, although cases of oral infection caused by the type 2 strain (HSV-2) are increasing. Herpes infections often present without symptoms. When symptoms do appear, they usually resolve within two weeks. The primary symptom of oral infection is inflammation of the mucosa of the cheeks and gums, a condition known as acute herpetic gingivostomatitis, which typically develops within 5 to 10 days of infection. Additional symptoms may include painful ulcers (sometimes mistaken for canker sores), fever, and sore throat. In adolescents, primary HSV infection often manifests as severe pharyngitis with lesions on the cheeks and gums. Some individuals may experience difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) and swollen lymph nodes (lymphadenopathy). In adults, primary HSV infections often result in pharyngitis resembling glandular fever (infectious mononucleosis), though gingivostomatitis is less common. Recurrent oral infections are more frequently associated with HSV-1 than HSV-2. Recurrences are often preceded by prodromal symptoms, such as tingling, itching, and redness of the skin around the infected site. Fluid-filled blisters eventually form on the lip (labial tissue) and the area between the lip and skin (vermilion border). This recurrent infection is commonly referred to as herpes simplex labialis. Rarely, reinfections may occur inside the mouth (intraoral HSV stomatitis), affecting the gums, alveolar ridge, hard palate, and the back of the tongue, sometimes accompanied by herpes labialis. Treatment for herpes labialis includes applying a cool, wet towel or ice to the sore to alleviate discomfort. Over-the-counter pain relievers such as ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) or acetaminophen (Tylenol) can help manage pain. Patients who experience significant pain may find it difficult to consume solid foods, but maintaining hydration is essential. Nutritional intake can be supported with fruit smoothies supplemented with protein powder. Vitamin supplements are also recommended. Citrus foods, such as tomatoes and lemons, should be avoided as they can exacerbate blister pain. Topical zinc oxide cream applied to the cold sore may help reduce the duration of the blister. Antiviral medications, such as acyclovir, have been used in some cases. For primary lesions, oral acyclovir or over-the-counter antiviral creams like Abreva (docosanol 10%) applied five times daily can help shorten the duration of symptoms.
